title: Grace, Mercy, and Peace
subtitle: 1–2 Timothy & Titus in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin:
These are letters from an older man to younger ones. Paul writes to Timothy in Ephesus and to Titus on Crete about elders and households, prayers and meals, widows keeping a lamp lit night and day. Then, from a prison in Rome, he writes once more to Timothy: remember your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, stir up the gift, I have finished the course, and please bring my cloak and the parchments before winter.

This book walks through them in forty short poems, in five parts: two for 1 Timothy, two for 2 Timothy, and one for Titus. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. The pictures stay with the things the letters touch—a rolled letter, a banked fire, a clay cup, a folded cloak—and leave the faces to your imagination.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open the letters to Timothy and Titus alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

paintings.title: my true child
paintings.epigraph: “to Timothy, my true child in faith”
paintings.poem:
he could have addressed it
to my assistant.
to my colleague.
to the man I left in charge.

he wrote
my true child.

some families
are made by birth.

some are made
by walking the same roads
long enough
that the older one's faith
starts to show
in the younger one's steps.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “my true child” (1 Timothy 1:2)—where the poem notes, “starts to show in the younger one's steps”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the goal
paintings.epigraph: “the goal of this command is love, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith”
paintings.poem:
there were men in Ephesus
arguing over family trees
and endless lists of names.

Paul cuts through it
in one line.

the point
was never to win.

the point
is love.

from a clean heart.
a clear conscience.
a faith with nothing to hide.

every rule, every sermon,
every late-night argument
is meant to end up there,

or it has lost the road.10
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the goal” (1 Timothy 1:3–5)—where the poem notes, “or it has lost the road.10”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the worst of them
paintings.epigraph: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.”
paintings.poem:
blasphemer.
persecutor.
insolent.

he lists it plainly,
like an old address.

then he writes
the surest sentence he knows:
Christ Jesus came
to save sinners,

of whom I am chief.

not was.
am.

if the first in line
was the worst in line,
then the line
is long enough
for you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the worst of them” (1 Timothy 1:15–16)—where the poem notes, “is long enough for you”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: shipwreck
paintings.epigraph: “holding faith and a good conscience”
paintings.poem:
Paul knew about ships.
he had seen more than one
go to pieces.

some, he warns,
thrust away a good conscience
and made shipwreck
of their faith.

not a storm
that came for them.
something they threw overboard
because it felt heavy.

hold on to it, Timothy.

it is ballast,
not burden.

it is what keeps you
upright
when the wind turns.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “shipwreck” (1 Timothy 1:18–19)—where the poem notes, “upright when the wind turns”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: for everyone
paintings.epigraph: “who desires all people to be saved and come to full knowledge of the truth.”
paintings.poem:
pray for everyone,
he says.
first of all.

for the emperor
who will never know your name.
for the magistrate.
for the neighbor
who knows it too well.

not because they're good.
because God
wants every one of them
saved.

the quiet life
starts here,
at a table,
holding up the names
of people
you would rather
argue with.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “for everyone” (1 Timothy 2:1–4)—where the poem notes, “you would rather argue with”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: one
paintings.epigraph: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus”
paintings.poem:
between the holy
and the ordinary.
between God
and someone like me.

there is not
a ladder
of better people.

there is not
a fee.

there is one man
standing in the gap,
the man Christ Jesus,

who gave himself
as a ransom for all.

one.
enough.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “one” (1 Timothy 2:5–6)—where the poem notes, “one. enough”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a pillar
paintings.epigraph: “the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.”
paintings.poem:
he hoped to come soon.
he wrote in case
he couldn't.

here is how to live,
he says,
in God's house.

and the house
isn't a building.

it's a few families
in someone's courtyard.
a lamp. a borrowed table.
people who don't agree
on much.

and God calls that
a pillar.

something
the truth
can stand on.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a pillar” (1 Timothy 3:14–15)—where the poem notes, “the truth can stand on”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the mystery
paintings.epigraph: “Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great”
paintings.poem:
it may have been a song
before it was a sentence.

revealed in the flesh.
justified in the spirit.
seen by angels.
preached among the nations.
believed on in the world.
received up in glory.

a mystery,
not because it's hidden,
but because it's
bigger than we are.

and it has
a name.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the mystery” (1 Timothy 3:16)—where the poem notes, “and it has a name”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: with thanksgiving
paintings.epigraph: “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving.”
paintings.poem:
some teachers
wanted a smaller table.
no this. no that.
holiness by subtraction.

Paul pulls the chairs
back in.

the bread is good.
the figs are good.
the wedding is good.
God made them.

what makes a meal holy
isn't what's missing from it.

it's the word of God,
and a prayer,
and open hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:3–5)—where the poem notes, “and a prayer, and open hands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: your youth
paintings.epigraph: “Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe”
paintings.poem:
too young,
someone must have said.

Paul doesn't tell him
to argue.
he doesn't tell him
to wait.

he says:
be the example.

in the way you talk.
the way you live.
in love. in faith.
in purity.

let them look
for a reason to dismiss you,

and find
a reason to follow.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 1 Timothy 4:12 (“and find a reason to follow”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: the lyre on the wall
paintings.epigraph: “Don’t neglect the gift that is in you”
paintings.poem:
there were hands on your head once.
older hands,
heavy and warm,
and words said over you
you may have
half forgotten.

the gift
didn't leave
when the hands lifted.

it's still there,
like a lyre on the wall
no one has tuned
in a while.

take it down.
give yourself to it.

let people see you
getting better.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were to set down one stone of remembrance today for how God has helped you thus far (1 Timothy 4:14–15), what would you name it?

paintings.title: night and day
paintings.epigraph: “she who is a widow indeed and desolate, has her hope set on God, and continues in petitions and prayers night and day.”
paintings.poem:
no one left
to cook for.
no one coming home.

the house is quiet now,
and she fills it
with names.

her hope set on God,
the letter says.
night and day.

honor her, Paul wrote.
see that she
never goes without.

some of the strongest work
in any city
happens in a small room,
by one lamp,
on two old knees.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “night and day” (1 Timothy 5:3–5)—where the poem notes, “by one lamp, on two old knees”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: a little wine
paintings.epigraph: “use a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities.”
paintings.poem:
in the middle of
instructions about elders,
witnesses, and warnings,

a line
only someone
who loved you
would write:

how is your stomach?
you're sick too often.
take care of yourself.

holiness
never asked you
to stop
having a body.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “a little wine” (1 Timothy 5:23)—where the poem notes, “to stop having a body”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: nothing in, nothing out
paintings.epigraph: “For we brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can’t carry anything out.”
paintings.poem:
you came in
with empty hands.

you'll go out
the same way.

in between:
a table,
a coat,
the people you love.

godliness with contentment,
he says,
is great gain.

not the gain
that fills a storeroom.

the gain
of not needing one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “nothing in, nothing out” (1 Timothy 6:6–8)—where the poem notes, “the gain of not needing one”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: unapproachable light
paintings.epigraph: “dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen, nor can see”
paintings.poem:
every emperor
put his face on a coin.

this King
has never been seen.
cannot be seen.

he lives in a light
no one can walk into.

the only Ruler.
King of kings.
owing his crown
to no one.

and still
his light spills over the ridge
and reaches
the valley
where we are.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What single step right in front of you is already lit by His word today, even if the far horizon remains unseen (1 Timothy 6:15–16)?

paintings.title: guard it
paintings.epigraph: “Timothy, guard that which is committed to you”
paintings.poem:
near the end
he calls him by name.

Timothy.

like a father at the door,
pressing something
into your hands:

this was given to you.
keep it.

not a treasure chest.
a trust.

don't trade it
for clever talk.

grace be with you.

and then the letter stops,
and the rest
is his to carry.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “guard it” (1 Timothy 6:20–21)—where the poem notes, “and the rest is his to carry”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: your tears
paintings.epigraph: “remembering your tears, that I may be filled with joy”
paintings.poem:
he remembers
the tears.

not the sermons.
not the miles.

the tears,
perhaps at a goodbye
neither of them wanted.

now the older man
prays for him
night and day,
longing to see him.

some of us are remembered
for what we built.

some of us
for who wept
when we left.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “your tears” (2 Timothy 1:3–4)—where the poem notes, “for who wept when we left”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: Lois and Eunice
paintings.epigraph: “the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice”
paintings.poem:
before it was his,
it lived at a table.

first in his grandmother, Lois.
then in his mother, Eunice.
then, Paul was sure of it,
in him.

no pulpit.
no title.
just a faith
with no pretending in it,

handed down
the way you hand down
a lamp,
still lit.

and a boy
was watching.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “Lois and Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5)—where the poem notes, “and a boy was watching”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: stir it up
paintings.epigraph: “stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.”
paintings.poem:
it isn't gone.
it's banked,
like a cook fire at dawn.
grey on top.
red underneath.

you don't need
a new fire.
you need to lean down
and breathe
on the one you have.

my hands were on your head,
Paul says.
I remember.

stir it up.

a gift from God
can go quiet.
it waits
for your breath.48
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In the quiet after the noise, what gentle truth from 2 Timothy 1:6 (“it waits for your breath.48”) is asking for your unhurried attention today?

paintings.title: not fear
paintings.epigraph: “For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”
paintings.poem:
the fear
came from somewhere.

not from him.

what he gave
was power
to stand,

love
to stay,

and a steady mind
to know
which one
this moment needs.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: What anxious weight can you place into the hands of the One who says, “Be still” and walks beside you in 2 Timothy 1:7?

paintings.title: I know him
paintings.epigraph: “I know him whom I have believed”
paintings.poem:
he doesn't say
I know what I believe.

he says
I know him.

a chain on his wrist.
everyone in Asia
turned away.

and what he has left,
he hands over
like a traveler
leaving his bag
with someone he trusts.

he isn't worried
about the bag.

he knows
the hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “I know him” (2 Timothy 1:12)—where the poem notes, “he knows the hands”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not ashamed of my chain
paintings.epigraph: “he often refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain”
paintings.poem:
Onesiphorus.
a name hardly anyone
can say.

he came to Rome
and looked for Paul.
kept looking
until he found him.

it isn't easy
to find a prisoner.
it's harder
to be seen with one.

he came anyway,
and more than once
he was fresh air
in that place.

may we be
the ones
who keep looking.54
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not ashamed of my chain” (2 Timothy 1:16–17)—where the poem notes, “the ones who keep looking.54”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: to others also
paintings.epigraph: “commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.”
paintings.poem:
Paul to Timothy.
Timothy to the faithful.
the faithful
to others also.

four hands
in one sentence.

nobody in that line
gets to be
the end of it.

somewhere back there,
someone handed it
to you.

look around.
whose hand
is open?
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “to others also” (2 Timothy 2:2)—where the poem notes, “whose hand is open?”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: not chained
paintings.epigraph: “But God’s word isn’t chained.”
paintings.poem:
remember Jesus Christ,
risen from the dead.

that's what he writes
from a cell.

they could lock the door.
they could fasten the iron.

but the words
had already left the room.

in letters.
in a young man's memory.
on roads
to places
Paul would never see.

the preacher
was chained.

the word
walked out.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “not chained” (2 Timothy 2:8–9)—where the poem notes, “the word walked out”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: faithful
paintings.epigraph: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful; for he can’t deny himself.”
paintings.poem:
we break.
he doesn't.

on our worst day
he is still
who he said he was.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “faithful” (2 Timothy 2:11–13)—where the poem notes, “he is still who he said he was”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: clay
paintings.epigraph: “he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work.”
paintings.poem:
in a large house
there are cups of gold and silver,
and cups of wood and clay.

you might think
the master always reaches
for the shiny one.

he reaches
for the clean one.

you don't have to be gold.

you have to be
ready.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “clay” (2 Timothy 2:20–21)—where the poem notes, “you have to be ready”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: from infancy
paintings.epigraph: “From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation”
paintings.poem:
stay with what you learned,
he says,
and remember
who you learned it from.

before you could read,
you heard it.

a voice at bedtime.
the old promises
said over you
like a blanket.

breathed out by God.
breathed in
by a child.

and still wise enough
to bring you
all the way home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “from infancy” (2 Timothy 3:14–16)—where the poem notes, “to bring you all the way home”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: fought, finished, kept
paintings.epigraph: “I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.”
paintings.poem:
he can see the end now.
already being poured out,
he writes,
like an offering.

no panic.
just three words
from a man at the end of the road:

fought.
finished.
kept.

then he looks past himself
to a crown
that isn't only his,
but for all
who have loved
his appearing.

it's the same
finish line.68
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “fought, finished, kept” (2 Timothy 4:6–8)—where the poem notes, “it's the same finish line.68”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the cloak and the parchments
paintings.epigraph: “Bring the cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus when you come, and the books, especially the parchments.”
paintings.poem:
after the crown
and the finish line,
this:

bring my cloak.
I left it at Troas.
and the books.
especially the parchments.

Demas has gone.
only Luke is with me.
bring Mark along.

the great apostle,
near the end,
wants a warm coat,
something to read,
and his friends.

that isn't
a smaller faith.
that is a whole one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “the cloak and the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:9–13) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: the Lord stood by me
paintings.epigraph: “But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me”
paintings.poem:
at my first defense
no one came.
everyone left.

he says it plainly.
and then:
may it not be
held against them.

and then:
but the Lord
stood by me.

when the room empties,
it isn't empty.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the Lord stood by me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17)—where the poem notes, “when the room empties, it isn't empty”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: before time began
paintings.epigraph: “in hope of eternal life, which God, who can’t lie, promised before time began”
paintings.poem:
a promise
made before there was
a morning
to make it in.

by the only one
who has never lied.

everything else in this letter,
the elders,
the households,
the hard work on Crete,

rests on that.

you can build a life
on a word
that old.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “before time began” (Titus 1:1–2)—where the poem notes, “on a word that old”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: the one who stays
paintings.epigraph: “I left you in Crete for this reason, that you would set in order the things that were lacking”
paintings.poem:
Paul sailed on.
Titus stayed.

stayed with the unfinished work,
the half-built things,
the towns with believers
and no elders yet.

set in order,
Paul told him,
what is still lacking.

not a glamorous job.

the job
of the one
who stays.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “the one who stays” (Titus 1:5)—where the poem notes, “of the one who stays”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: an open door
paintings.epigraph: “given to hospitality, a lover of good”
paintings.poem:
the list for leaders
isn't long on talent.

not quick-tempered.
not greedy.
not violent.

and then:
given to hospitality.

in God's house
a leader is someone
whose own door
is open,

whose table
always has room
for one more.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you pause at the threshold of “an open door” (Titus 1:7–8), what closed place in your life is waiting for you to open to His presence?

paintings.title: to the pure
paintings.epigraph: “To the pure, all things are pure”
paintings.poem:
the same field
at sunrise.

one heart sees
a thing to grab.

another sees
a thing to thank God for.

it isn't the field
that's different.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “to the pure” (Titus 1:15)—where the poem notes, “it isn't the field that's different”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: teachers of what is good
paintings.epigraph: “teachers of that which is good”
paintings.poem:
no pulpit here either.
a kitchen.
a courtyard.

the older women,
Paul says,
are teachers
of what is good.

not lecturers.
teachers,
the way one hand
shows another
how to work the dough.

how to love.
how to be kind
when the day is long.

it comes from someone
who has done it,
beside you.84
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “teachers of what is good” (Titus 2:3–4)—where the poem notes, “who has done it, beside you.84”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: grace has appeared
paintings.epigraph: “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men”
paintings.poem:
grace didn't arrive
as an idea.

it appeared,
the way morning appears
over the edge of the sea,
all at once,
and for everyone.

and it teaches us,
the letter says.
to say no
to what ruins us.
to live
sober, upright, godly,
right here
in this present age.

grace came once.

we are watching
the horizon
for its appearing.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “grace has appeared” (Titus 2:11–13) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?

paintings.title: his own
paintings.epigraph: “purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.”
paintings.poem:
he gave himself
to buy us back.

not to make us
names on a list,

but a people
he calls
his own.

and people
who are held like that
get restless
to do good.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “his own” (Titus 2:14)—where the poem notes, “get restless to do good”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: we too
paintings.epigraph: “But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared”
paintings.poem:
we too,
Paul says.
not you.
we.

foolish once.
led around by what we wanted.
envious.
hating,
and hated.

that's who we were
when kindness
walked in.

not because of anything
we had done.
because of his mercy.

so be gentle
with the ones
still standing
where you stood.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “we too” (Titus 3:2–5)—where the poem notes, “still standing where you stood”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: poured out richly
paintings.epigraph: “the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly”
paintings.poem:
washed.
made new.
poured out on.

not a few drops
measured to what we deserved.

a jar
tipped
all the way over.

richly.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As you linger with “poured out richly” (Titus 3:5–6)—where the poem notes, “richly”—where do you recognize this same moment on your own walk today?

paintings.title: grace be with you all
paintings.epigraph: “Grace be with you all.”
paintings.poem:
the last lines
are travel plans.

come to me at Nicopolis.
I've decided to winter there.
send Zenas and Apollos on their way,
and see that they lack nothing.

still planning.
still sending.
still making sure
the ones on the road
have what they need.

then the word
he never forgets
to end with.

grace.

to Timothy.
to Titus.
to all of you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: How does the mercy shown in “grace be with you all” (Titus 3:12–15) change the way you look at your own weakness—or at someone who needs your grace today?
